foot and mouth.what_to_do: Isolate affected animals immediately. Contact your nearest vet or DVS office. Do not move animals off the farm. Report to authorities — FMD is a notifiable disease.
foot and mouth.symptoms: Blisters on hooves, mouth, and tongue. Excessive salivation, lameness, reduced milk production.
foot and mouth.prevention: Vaccination, restrict animal movement, biosecurity measures.

goat pox.what_to_do: Isolate affected animals. Contact a vet for antiviral treatment. Vaccinate healthy animals in the herd.
goat pox.symptoms: Raised skin nodules, fever, nasal discharge, difficulty breathing.
goat pox.prevention: Annual vaccination, quarantine new animals, avoid contact with infected herds.

healthy cattle.what_to_do: Your animal appears healthy. Continue regular monitoring, vaccination schedules, and good nutrition.
healthy cattle.prevention: Maintain regular vet checkups, vaccination, and clean water and feed.

healthy goat.what_to_do: Your goat appears healthy. Continue regular monitoring and good husbandry practices.
healthy goat.prevention: Maintain regular vet checkups, vaccination, and clean water and feed.

lumpy cow disease.what_to_do: Isolate affected animals. Contact a vet for supportive treatment. Vaccinate the rest of the herd. Control insects around the farm.
lumpy cow disease.symptoms: Raised skin nodules across the body, fever, nasal discharge, reduced milk production, swollen lymph nodes.
lumpy cow disease.prevention: Annual vaccination, insect control, quarantine new animals.

watermelon mosaic virus.what_to_do: Remove and destroy infected plants. Control aphid populations with insecticide. Do not plant cucurbits near infected areas.
watermelon mosaic virus.symptoms: Mottled yellow-green mosaic on leaves, distorted fruit, stunted growth.
watermelon mosaic virus.prevention: Use virus-resistant varieties, control aphids, remove weeds around the field.

healthy watermelon.what_to_do: Your plant appears healthy. Continue regular monitoring, irrigation, and fertilisation.
healthy watermelon.prevention: Maintain crop rotation, control pests, ensure proper irrigation.

sorghum cereal grain mold.what_to_do: Harvest early before full maturity in wet seasons. Dry grain quickly after harvest. Use fungicide if caught early.
sorghum cereal grain mold.symptoms: Pink, red, or black discolouration on grain heads, shrivelled grain.
sorghum cereal grain mold.prevention: Use mould-resistant varieties, avoid delayed harvest, improve field drainage.

potato late blight.what_to_do: Apply fungicide immediately. Remove and destroy infected plant material. Avoid overhead irrigation.
potato late blight.symptoms: Water-soaked dark lesions on leaves and stems, white mould on undersides of leaves, rotting tubers.
potato late blight.prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply preventive fungicide, avoid wet conditions.

tomato late blight.what_to_do: Apply fungicide immediately. Remove and destroy infected plant material. Avoid overhead irrigation.
tomato late blight.symptoms: Dark water-soaked lesions on leaves and fruit, white mould growth, rapid plant collapse.
tomato late blight.prevention: Use resistant varieties, apply preventive fungicide, improve air circulation.

healthy potato.what_to_do: Your plant appears healthy. Continue regular monitoring and good crop management.
healthy potato.prevention: Maintain crop rotation, control pests, ensure proper irrigation.

healthy tomato.what_to_do: Your plant appears healthy. Continue regular monitoring and good crop management.
healthy tomato.prevention: Maintain crop rotation, control pests, ensure proper irrigation.

african swine fever.symptoms: High fever, loss of appetite, red or purple blotching on skin, vomiting, diarrhea, sudden death.
african swine fever.spreads_by: Direct contact with infected pigs, contaminated feed or equipment, ticks (soft ticks of the Ornithodoros genus), and swill feeding.
african swine fever.what_to_do: Report immediately to a state veterinarian — this is a notifiable disease. There is no cure or approved vaccine, so affected herds are typically quarantined and culled to stop spread.
african swine fever.prevention: Avoid swill feeding, control pig movement, disinfect equipment and vehicles between farms, and report sick or dead pigs promptly.

newcastle disease.symptoms: Respiratory distress, greenish diarrhea, twisted neck or paralysis, drop in egg production, sudden death in severe outbreaks.
newcastle disease.affects: Poultry — chickens are most susceptible; also affects other birds.
newcastle disease.spreads_by: Direct contact with infected birds, contaminated droppings, equipment, feed, water, and airborne transmission over short distances.
newcastle disease.what_to_do: Isolate sick birds immediately and contact a veterinarian. There is no treatment; vaccination is the primary control measure once an outbreak is confirmed.
newcastle disease.prevention: Vaccinate flocks on schedule, restrict visitor access to poultry housing, disinfect equipment, and quarantine new birds before introducing them to the flock.

brucellosis.symptoms: Abortion in late pregnancy, retained placenta, reduced fertility, swollen joints; often no obvious symptoms outside pregnancy.
brucellosis.affects: Cattle, goats, sheep, and pigs. Can also infect humans (zoonotic) through contact with infected animals, birth fluids, or unpasteurized milk.
brucellosis.spreads_by: Contact with aborted fetuses, placenta, and birth fluids; contaminated milk; breeding with infected animals.
brucellosis.what_to_do: Isolate aborting animals, avoid handling birth material with bare hands, and contact a veterinarian for testing. Infected animals are usually culled as part of control programs.
brucellosis.prevention: Vaccinate calves/kids where a national program is in place, test and remove infected animals, and pasteurize milk before consumption.

anthrax.symptoms: Sudden death is often the first sign; also fever, difficulty breathing, staggering, and bleeding from body openings (nose, mouth, anus) after death.
anthrax.affects: Cattle, sheep, goats, and other grazing livestock. Zoonotic — can infect humans through contact with infected carcasses or products.
anthrax.spreads_by: Ingestion of spores from contaminated soil or pasture, especially after soil disturbance or flooding in endemic areas.
anthrax.what_to_do: Do NOT open or perform a post-mortem on a carcass suspected of anthrax — this releases spores. Report immediately to a veterinarian for confirmation and safe carcass disposal (burning or deep burial with lime).
anthrax.prevention: Vaccinate livestock in known endemic areas, avoid grazing on land with a history of anthrax deaths, and dispose of carcasses safely and promptly.

blackleg.symptoms: Sudden lameness, swelling in the hindquarters or shoulder that crackles under the skin (gas under the skin), high fever, sudden death, often in well-conditioned young cattle.
blackleg.affects: Young cattle (6 months to 2 years) primarily; occasionally sheep.
blackleg.spreads_by: Caused by soil-borne Clostridium bacteria that enter through wounds or are ingested; spores can survive in soil for years.
blackleg.what_to_do: Contact a veterinarian promptly — antibiotics may help if caught very early, but the disease progresses rapidly and is often fatal. Vaccination of the remaining herd is recommended after an outbreak.
blackleg.prevention: Vaccinate young cattle annually in areas with a history of blackleg, and avoid grazing on land where previous cases have occurred.

heartwater.symptoms: High fever, loss of appetite, nervous signs including circling, high-stepping gait, and convulsions; fluid buildup around the heart and lungs.
heartwater.spreads_by: Bite of infected bont ticks (Amblyomma species).
heartwater.what_to_do: Contact a veterinarian for antibiotic treatment (tetracyclines) as soon as symptoms appear — early treatment improves survival chances significantly.
heartwater.prevention: Regular tick control through dipping or acaricide treatment, and pasture management to reduce tick populations.

maize streak virus.symptoms: Narrow, broken yellow-white streaks running parallel to leaf veins; stunted growth and poor cob development in severe cases.
maize streak virus.affects: Maize, and to a lesser extent other cereal grasses.
maize streak virus.spreads_by: Leafhoppers (Cicadulina species), which pick up the virus from infected plants and spread it as they feed on healthy ones.
maize streak virus.what_to_do: Remove and destroy severely infected plants where practical. There is no cure once a plant is infected — focus shifts to protecting the rest of the field.
maize streak virus.prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant maize varieties, control leafhopper populations, and avoid staggered planting near older infected maize fields.

groundnut rosette.symptoms: Stunted, bushy plants with distorted growing shoots; yellowing or mottling of leaves; little to no pod formation if infected while young.
groundnut rosette.spreads_by: Aphids (Aphis craccivora), which transmit the virus complex as they feed; can spread rapidly through a field within weeks.
groundnut rosette.what_to_do: Remove and destroy infected plants early to slow spread. There is no chemical cure once a plant is infected.
groundnut rosette.prevention: Plant early and at higher density (aphids prefer sparse, late-planted crops), use resistant varieties where available, and control aphid populations with appropriate insecticides.

cassava mosaic disease.symptoms: Yellow-green mosaic pattern on leaves, leaf distortion and curling, stunted plant growth, reduced tuber (root) yield.
cassava mosaic disease.spreads_by: Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) and the use of infected cuttings for planting.
cassava mosaic disease.what_to_do: Remove and destroy infected plants. Always source planting material (cuttings) from certified disease-free stock rather than an infected field.
cassava mosaic disease.prevention: Plant resistant varieties, use clean/certified cuttings, and control whitefly populations.

sorghum anthracnose.symptoms: Small red, tan, or black spots on leaves that enlarge and merge; reddish discoloration on stalks; grain mold on infected heads in humid conditions.
sorghum anthracnose.spreads_by: Fungal spores spread by wind, rain splash, and infected crop residue left in the field.
sorghum anthracnose.what_to_do: Remove and destroy infected crop residue after harvest. Fungicide treatment can help in severe outbreaks — consult an extension officer for locally approved products.
sorghum anthracnose.prevention: Plant resistant varieties, rotate crops away from sorghum for a season, and avoid dense planting that keeps foliage wet for longer periods.
